newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain employers, unions to struggle on with talks.
newsitem.headline: Spain employers, unions to struggle on with talks.

text.p: Spain's employers and unions return to the negotiating table on Wednesday seeking to break the deadlock in labour talks and secure a deal on key reforms before the government imposes its own measures.
After days of intensive talks, the two sides reached stalemate on the key issue of contracts for young workers and temporarily broke off negotiations last Thursday to chew over new proposals.

The government had given unions and employers until early March to reach a deal before it would step in and impose a package. But, aware of the prickly nature of the issues, it said it would be patient.
"We expect an accord will be reached as soon as possible and the government will not interfere in the speed of talks," Labour Minister Javier Arenas told reporters on Monday.
"Only when the talks have completely broken down will the government directly intervene."

Struggling to cut the European Union's highest unemployment rate, the government is keen to secure an agreement to liberalise the rigid labour market and prepare the economy for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Employers and unions remain optimistic that they will eventually reach an agreement.
"There have been advances in all areas, none of which we have permanently shut the door on," Antonio Gutierrez, leader of the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) union, told local radio.
The key sticking point now lies in contracts for young workers, the main victims of unemployment in Spain.
The employers' latest proposal centres on a permanent contract aimed at young jobless people up to the age of 27. Unions want even more contract stability.
But even if a deal is reached, one leading union said it doubted whether it would do much to reduce Spain's 22 percent unemployment rate.
"The employers' proposals will deepen the precariousness of jobs that we currently have," Antonio Ordonez, spokesman for the General Workers' union (UGT), told local media on Sunday.
At the same time, analysts fear that if a deal is not reached, the government would fail to be as radical in its reforms as it has promised.
The government knows, however, that an accord needs to be voluntary to be truly effective.
Unions warned last week that government-imposed reforms would fail and lead to labour disputes.
Previous attempts to impose reforms have had little success and liberalisation measures enforced in 1994 by the previous Socialist administration sparked a 24-hour strike.
